title: Pick two or pick four
hook: Six friends, one trip. Is there more choice in taking 2 or in taking 4?

doesNotKnow: that choosing k of n has exactly as many ways as choosing the n − k left behind, because each choice of who goes is a choice of who stays

misconception: Choosing 4 of 6 gives more possible groups than choosing 2 of 6, because the groups are bigger.
objective: The learner can say that taking 2 of 6 friends and taking 4 of 6 give the same number of groups, 15, because each pair that goes leaves exactly one group of four that stays, and the other way round.

claims.text: From 6 friends there are 15 ways to choose 2 and 15 ways to choose 4; there are 20 ways to choose 3, the most of any group size. Recall: from 10 players there are 45 ways to pick 2 and 45 ways to pick 8.
claims.source: company/domains/briefs/checks/math-wave-j-check.mjs label D5: C(6,0..6) = 1, 6, 15, 20, 15, 6, 1; C(10,2) = C(10,8) = 45. Stage: subsets(6, k) in Demo.tsx enumerates every group, and the counters and 'groups of 3: 20' are its lengths.

claims.text: Matching each chosen group with the group left out is one to one: every pair of the 6 leaves exactly one four behind, and every four is left behind by exactly one pair, so choosing k of n has as many ways as choosing n − k. Each chip on the stage shows a pair (filled dots) and the four it leaves (hollow dots).
claims.source: Bijection: the map 'group → its complement' is its own inverse, so it is one to one and onto between k-subsets and (n − k)-subsets; C(n, k) = C(n, n − k). Stage: Demo.tsx checks at load that the 15 complements of the pairs are 15 different fours covering every four.

recall.question: A coach has 10 players. She can pick 2 to rest, or pick 8 to play. Which choice has more possible picks?
recall.why: Each 2 who rest leaves exactly one 8 who play, and the other way round, so both have the same number of picks: 45.
